DC CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING
OBJECTIVES
w Determine if a DM transmitter and receiver system is operating correctly.
w Identify the faulted component in a malfunctioning DM transmitter and receiver system.......................
. The experiment in this lesson is not setup to use the selected trainer.
EQUIPMENT REQUIRED
Definition
In this lesson, you will troubleshoot faults in a DM transmitter and receiver system.
INTRODUCTIONM
Troubleshooting DM systems is not difficult due to the use of only one major integrated circuit.
Measuring the input and output signals of a chip determines if the chip is faulted. That's all there is to it!
However, there is support circuitry in the DM system that could cause the main modulator/demodulator chip to appear faulted.
So, you must first isolate the malfunctioning DM system to either the transmitter or the receiver.
In other words, you troubleshoot a DM system as you would any signal processing system. You isolate the fault from the system down to a circuit!
Let's begin the lesson on DM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING......................

DM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING
In this experiment, you will locate the failed chip or component in a DM transmitter and receiver system.
EXPERIMENT
PC130-332 SCHEMATIC - Transmitter
The transmitter consists of a MC3418 CVSD modulator and support circuitry.
PC130-333 SCHEMATIC - Receiver
The receiver consists of a MC3418 CVSD demodulator and support circuitry.
To locate a faulted chip, you must first determine if the DM system is operating correctly.
This is accomplished by making one simple oscilloscope measurement. Measure the input to the transmitter and the output of the receiver.
If the output signal matches the input signal, the DM system is operating correctly.
If you do not have a good signal on the output of the receiver, the system is faulted.
Once you have determined that the DM system is not operating correctly you must then isolate the fault to either the transmitter, transmission medium or receiver.
This is accomplished by making two simple oscilloscope measurements.
First, measure the output of the transmitter.
If a DM signal is present, the transmitter circuit must be operating correctly.
If the DM signal is not present, the transmitter is faulted.
Second, measure the input to the receiver. You already know that the receiver has a bad output or you would not be troubleshooting the system.
If an attenuated DM signal is not present on the input, the fault is in the transmission medium.
If an attenuated DM signal is present on the output, the fault is in the receiver.
If the fault is in the transmission medium, checking out the antenna or transmission cables will normally locate the failure.
If the fault is in the transmitter, oscilloscope measurements will isolate the fault to circuit.
If the fault is in the receiver, oscilloscope measurements will isolate the fault to a circuit.

PC130-333 SCHEMATIC - Receiver

3. Determine the faulted circuit in the transmitter by measuring the signals on the IC pins and TPs of PC130-332. Which circuit in the transmitter is faulted?
The signal on IC1 pin 9 is correct, output of modulator. The signal is an inverted DM signal. The modulator is not faulted.
TRY AGAIN!
The signal TP2 is correct. The clock circuit of IC2c and IC2b is not faulted.
TRY AGAIN!
The signal on TPs 3, 5 and 6 are correct. The filters are not faulted.
TRY AGAIN!
Which IC or component is most likely to cause the fault?
You should have measured a correct signal on IC1 pin 9, output of modulator. This indicates that IC1 is operating correctly.
TRY AGAIN!

TRY AGAIN!
Congratulations, you determined that the fault is the output inverter, IC2a.
In this case, IC2a was not receiving an input.
The computer will now remove the fault. Check the output of the receiver on PC130-333 TP6 and verify the DM system is operating correctly.
